results.describe: Origin, rate limit, proof-of-work, body parse and the outbound fetch still run in that order.

findings.title: The protocol allowlist is unreachable for any scheme that does not start with the letters "http"
findings.detail: app/scan-url/route.ts:200 does `new URL(url.startsWith("http") ? url : `https://${url}`)`. A `file:` URL does not start with "http", so it is rewritten into `https://file:///etc/passwd` — an https URL whose hostname is the word "file". The `["http:","https:"]` check four lines later then sees "https:" and passes. The scheme was not rejected; it was renamed into a hostname, and that single-label hostname is handed to the resolver. On a host with a DNS search suffix a single label is not nothing, and the check that was supposed to stop this never ran. The resolve-then-judge guard below still refuses a private answer, which is why this is low rather than an SSRF.
findings.evidence: POST /scan-url {"url":"file:///etc/passwd"} with a valid proof-of-work => 200; resolver was asked for ["file"]; 1 outbound request(s) made
findings.remediation: Parse the URL once with no rewrite, and only prepend https:// when the string contains no "://" at all. Then the protocol allowlist sees the real scheme.

results.describe: Error bodies carry a fixed string and nothing else, and /ip reflects no unbounded caller input.

findings.title: /ip reflects unbounded caller-supplied geo headers back in its response
findings.detail: app/ip/route.ts decodeHeader() returns x-geo-city / -region / -country / -timezone verbatim, with no length bound. Nothing on the droplet sets these and the vhost strips only the four IP headers, so in production every value here is the caller's own input coming back. It is self-inflicted and the response is no-store, so there is no victim other than the sender — but the same buildIpResponse also answers /dns-leak/start, and countryCode is handed to Intl.DisplayNames, so an unbounded string is being carried further than it needs to be.
findings.evidence: POST /ip with x-geo-city: "A"×4096 => 200 with city length 4096
findings.remediation: Bound each geo field to something a place name fits in (64-128 characters) inside decodeHeader, and drop values that exceed it rather than truncating into a half-name. Adding x-geo-* to the vhost's RequestHeader unset list would close it at the proxy too.

findings.title: getRedisDiagnostic is dead code whose comment invites someone to wire it up
findings.detail: lib/rate-limit.ts:66 exports getRedisDiagnostic() and documents it as "surfaced via response headers". It has no caller anywhere in app/ or lib/. Guarding a dead hazard with a test is the cheaper-looking option that leaves the hazard in the tree: the next person to debug a Redis problem finds an exported helper whose comment tells them to put its output in a response.
findings.evidence: scanned 82 .ts/.tsx files under app/ and lib/; getRedisDiagnostic( appears at no call site
findings.remediation: Delete the export. getRedisStatus() covers the one thing a route legitimately needs to know.

results.describe: Both /dns-leak routes gate on Origin, validate the test id, and do not distinguish an unknown id from an unpolled one.
Preflights give a foreign origin no ACAO, mirror the real origin exactly, and never allow credentials.
The live API derives the rate-limiting client IP from the proxy, not from a header the caller sent.
No API route module exports an HTTP verb beyond POST and OPTIONS.
A client-supplied Host cannot satisfy the Origin allowlist on any of the six gated routes.

findings.title: The Origin gate accepts any origin whose host matches the client-supplied Host header
findings.detail: Apache runs ProxyPreserveHost On, so the Host header reaching Node is written by the caller. lib/origin.ts treats Origin.host === Host as same-origin and allows it, so a caller sets both to the same fabricated value and is inside. The allowlist is never consulted. The routes still refuse a foreign Origin sent with the REAL Host, which is why the source-grep tests and the live smoke both report green: they only ever send the real Host. Proof-of-work, rate limiting and the SSRF guards are unaffected — this is the outermost filter, not the load-bearing one, hence low. Note the responses also mirror the fabricated origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which is harmless only because a browser cannot set Host.
findings.evidence: isOriginAllowed("https://evil.example", "evil.example") => true (expected false) | isOriginAllowed("https://evil.example:8443", "evil.example:8443") => true (expected false) | POST /challenge with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example | POST /scan-url with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 401, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example | POST /ip with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example | POST /event with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 400, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example | POST /dns-leak/start with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example | POST /dns-leak/result with Origin: https://evil.example + Host: evil.example => 400, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example
findings.remediation: Drop the same-origin shortcut in isOriginAllowed and rely on the allowlist alone. That change MUST land with ALLOWED_ORIGINS containing the API's own origin (https://206-189-186-34.nip.io — already recorded at API-ON-DROPLET.md:115), or the site stops being able to call itself. Gate the deploy on scripts/security-smoke.mjs section B, which is the canary for exactly that.

results.describe: Proof-of-work tokens cannot be extended, re-pointed at another challenge, truncated or re-typed.
A solved proof-of-work buys exactly one scan even when the replay store is unreachable.
/stats refuses every near-miss bearer, never emits CORS headers, and bounds its day parameter and body.
The live .htaccess managed block still matches scripts/droplet-htaccess.conf, the vhost still strips forged client-IP headers and caps bodies, and the config still parses.

findings.title: 18 .htaccess.bak.* copies are sitting in the web root
findings.detail: droplet-server-config.sh writes one on every run and removes none. Each is a complete old security-header block, one `cp` away from being the live one — including versions whose CSP named two origins that will become registerable by strangers. They are also in a directory Apache serves, and only the stock `.ht*` rule keeps them from being fetched.
findings.evidence: ls -1 /var/www/html/.htaccess.bak.* | wc -l → 18 (warn at 6)
findings.remediation: Keep the newest one or two and delete the rest; better, have droplet-server-config.sh write them outside the DocumentRoot.

results.describe: Every vhost that proxies /api/ still logs those requests without the client address — the "we count clicks, not people" promise, as config.

findings.title: Graded 1 vhost(s) that proxy /api/
findings.detail: Vhosts that do not proxy /api/ are deliberately out of scope — their logging is the team's WordPress configuration, which this project has no authority over.
findings.evidence: sites-enabled proxying /api/: /etc/apache2/sites-enabled/000-default-le-ssl.conf; all enabled: 000-default-le-ssl.conf, 000-default.conf

results.describe: The root deploy credential on this machine — .secrets and the ssh key it names — is 0600, encrypted at rest, and outside the repo.

findings.title: The root deploy key has no passphrase
findings.detail: At rest it is a plain root credential for the production box. The realistic path here is not a stolen laptop — it is this repo: a malicious postinstall during `npm ci` reads ~/.ssh and has root on the box that serves the team's WordPress. A passphrase plus ssh-agent costs one prompt per session and makes the file useless on its own.
findings.evidence: /Users/davidshadrake/.ssh/id_ed25519: OpenSSH private key with cipher "none" (read from the first 512 bytes; no key material is reproduced here)
findings.remediation: ssh-keygen -p -f /Users/davidshadrake/.ssh/id_ed25519 to add a passphrase, then ssh-add it once per session. Better still, issue a non-root deploy user with a narrower authorized_keys command.

results.describe: The root filesystem has bytes and inodes to spare, and log rotation is still bounded by size — the pair that stops an API flood from taking MySQL down.

findings.title: /var/log/apache2 is 3 MB
findings.detail: Context for the headroom numbers above. A sudden jump here is what a flood looks like from the disk's point of view, and it is the first place to look when / starts filling.
findings.evidence: du -sm /var/log/apache2 → 3	/var/log/apache2

results.describe: /etc/ib-api.env is not readable beyond root — and the standing fact that www-data, the WordPress uid, can read it.

findings.title: /etc/ib-api.env is readable by the www-data group — the same uid as the team's WordPress
findings.detail: This is the current, intended arrangement and not a regression: the systemd unit runs as www-data and has to read the file. It is graded as a standing warning because the cost is real — any file-read bug in the co-hosted WordPress yields both secrets — and because a warning is what keeps the fix on the table. systemd LoadCredential= (or a dedicated ib-api uid) removes www-data from the picture without changing how the service starts.
findings.evidence: stat -c '%n %U %G %a' /etc/ib-api.env → root www-data 640
findings.remediation: Move the two secrets to systemd credentials: LoadCredential=ib-api-env:/etc/ib-api.env with the file 0600 root:root, or give ib-api its own uid and chown the file to it.

results.describe: Redis, MySQL and the Node API still bind loopback only, and nothing unexpected answers on a public address.
Pending SECURITY updates, a pending reboot, and whether unattended-upgrades is still enabled on the one box that exists.

findings.title: 1 pending security update
findings.detail: There is one box and no staging. A security update sitting here is sitting on the team's WordPress and MySQL as much as on our tools. Threshold for high is 5.
findings.evidence: /usr/lib/update-notifier/apt-check --human-readable → Expanded Security Maintenance for Applications is not enabled. |  | 61 updates can be applied immediately. | 1 of these updates is a standard security update. | To see these additional updates run: apt list --upgradable |  | Enable ESM Apps to receive additional future security updates. | See https: (of 61 updates total)
findings.remediation: apt-get update && apt-get upgrade, at a time when a brief Apache/MySQL restart is acceptable. Check `apt list --upgradable` first for anything that restarts the database.

findings.title: The box is running code it no longer has on disk — a reboot is pending
findings.detail: Something (usually a kernel or a core library) has been upgraded and the running processes still hold the old version. Until the reboot, the patch that was applied is not in effect, so the apt state reads clean while the vulnerability is still live. On a single host with no failover this needs a scheduled window, not a nightly surprise.
findings.evidence: test -f /var/run/reboot-required → REBOOT_REQUIRED
findings.remediation: Schedule a reboot. Confirm ib-api, apache2, mysql and redis-server are all enabled first (api-unit-resource-ceilings grades that for ib-api).

findings.title: Host: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS · kernel 6.8.0-71-generic
findings.detail: Reported every night so an approaching LTS end-of-life is visible long before it is urgent. Not graded — the upgrade is a scheduled project, not a nightly failure.
findings.evidence: lsb_release -ds; uname -r → Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS | 6.8.0-71-generic

results.describe: sshd still refuses passwords and permits root by key only — the pair that keeps the one internet-facing management port out of reach of a credential-stuffing run.

findings.title: PermitRootLogin is yes, not prohibit-password
findings.detail: Not exploitable as it stands: password and keyboard-interactive authentication are both off, so root is reachable by key only in practice. What it costs is the second layer. The whole protection now rests on one directive in a file that package upgrades and cloud-init both write to — restore password authentication by accident and root becomes guessable in the same moment, with nothing else to stop it. `prohibit-password` makes that impossible rather than merely unlikely.
findings.evidence: sshd -T → permitrootlogin yes, passwordauthentication no, kbdinteractiveauthentication no
findings.remediation: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password. Deploys keep working: .secrets uses key authentication as root already, and prohibit-password permits exactly that.

findings.title: fail2ban: inactive / not-found
findings.detail: Reported, never graded. With password authentication off, fail2ban mostly trims log noise rather than closing a path in, and a nightly line recommending software nobody decided to install is how a suite gets muted.
findings.evidence: systemctl is-active fail2ban; systemctl is-enabled fail2ban → inactive / not-found; sshd port 22

findings.title: ib-api runs as www-data, the same uid as Apache and WordPress PHP
findings.detail: Recorded here as context for the sandbox properties above. The durable fix is a dedicated uid (or DynamicUser= with LoadCredential= for /etc/ib-api.env), which would also take www-data out of the picture for the secrets file. Graded by webroot-ownership-shared-fate and env-secret-file-perms, not here.
findings.evidence: systemctl show ib-api -p User → User=www-data

findings.title: 9 statutory request-letter templates state law with no not-legal-advice line
findings.detail: Each of these hands the reader a letter to send to a real company, telling them a controller must respond within a stated period or citing a statute by number. That is a statement of law being relied on, not editorial. components/TemplatePage.tsx has no disclaimer slot at all, so there is currently nowhere to put one — which is why this is one structural fix rather than 23 edits. data/templates/ccpa/ccpa-california-privacy-request-letter-template.json — states a deadline the reader is told the law sets: "within 45 days"; cites Section 1798.130
data/templates/cloud-privacy/cloud-storage-privacy-request-letter-template.json — cites Article 15
data/templates/dating-privacy/dating-app-privacy-request-letter-template.json — cites Article 15

results.describe: A privacy notice page exists and is linked from every built page, and every tool that sends something to the API discloses what it sends (GDPR Art. 13 notice at collection).

findings.title: No privacy notice page exists on either site
findings.detail: The API receives the visitor's IP on /ip, /scan-url and /event, and lib/dns-leak-store.ts persists their full public IP in Redis for 600 seconds. GDPR/UK GDPR Art. 13 requires that to be disclosed at the point of collection, and these sites are globally reachable and specifically address EU readers. There is nowhere on either site that says what is collected, why, for how long, or who runs it. This is not a hard fix — one page and one footer link — and it is the only clearly binding compliance duty on this project that is currently unmet.
findings.evidence:
searched 28 page routes under app/ for a privacy/privacy-notice/privacy-policy route: none found
the nearest thing is app/site/methodology/page.tsx, which explains how OTHER sites are scanned, not what we collect
findings.remediation: Add app/privacy/page.tsx covering: the public IP received by /ip, /scan-url, /event and /dns-leak/start; the 600-second Redis retention in lib/dns-leak-store.ts; the counters behind /stats; that there are no cookies and no third-party loads; and who the controller is. Then link it from the footer in app/layout.tsx.

findings.title: Tool sends data to the server with no registered disclosure: components/tools/DnsLeakTestTool.tsx
findings.detail: This component calls the scan API, so something leaves the visitor's browser and reaches our server — at minimum their IP, and usually a URL they typed. Nothing in the tool tells them that. GDPR Art. 13 wants the disclosure where the collection happens, and it is also simply what this product says it stands for.
findings.evidence: components/tools/DnsLeakTestTool.tsx matches 3 API-dependency pattern(s) and has no entry in scripts/security/data/compliance-disclosures.json
findings.remediation: Render one sentence near the control that starts the request, saying what is sent and what the server does with it — CookieAnalyzerTool.tsx's "Scan has our server load the page… The site sees a visit from our server." is the model. Then register it in compliance-disclosures.json.

results.describe: The export on the droplet is a known, committed, on-main build — so the source-level content guards are describing the pages people actually read.

findings.title: The free tier is running a commit that is not on origin/main: 9f8842e
findings.detail: The live build came from a branch or a detached commit that never reached origin/main. Review, CI and every content guard run against main; a build off main has had none of them applied to it in any binding way.
findings.evidence: live sha 9f8842e; `git merge-base --is-ancestor 9f8842e origin/main` is false

findings.title: The pro tier is running a commit that is not on origin/main: 9f8842e
findings.detail: The live build came from a branch or a detached commit that never reached origin/main. Review, CI and every content guard run against main; a build off main has had none of them applied to it in any binding way.
findings.evidence: live sha 9f8842e; `git merge-base --is-ancestor 9f8842e origin/main` is false

results.describe: The Pro folder holds a real Pro build, not a second copy of the free site — which version.txt cannot tell you, because both tiers are stamped from one variable.
No route sets a cookie, and every localStorage/sessionStorage key carries a written "strictly necessary" justification — the two facts that keep this site consent-exempt.
No third-party script, stylesheet, image, iframe or font in the built export — the property that keeps the site consent-exempt and stops a tracking pixel img-src would allow.
Every upgrade CTA in the built pages resolves to Google Play or the app's own upgrade screen, or to a declared exception with a named owner and an end date.
A temporary override can actually be turned off: it is declared with an owner and an end date, and no test pins its current value where the rollback would break.
All seven API routes refuse every verb but their own, and no response body discloses the droplet's filesystem layout or plumbing.
Garbage input to every route (bad JSON, null, wrong content-type, a lying Content-Length) returns a small JSON error, never a stack trace or a filesystem path.
Dotfiles, config, backups and source maps under the two site roots and the shared web root are not served.
Every security header the repo declares is served live, with the exact declared value, on pages, tool pages, the Pro site, a hashed asset and the API.
Plain http redirects to the configured https host, and a forged Host / X-Forwarded-Host cannot redirect a visitor somewhere else.

findings.title: Known and accepted: a scripted client can satisfy the origin gate with a matching forged Host and Origin
findings.detail: isOriginAllowed() returns true when the Origin's host equals the request's Host header, which is what lets the deployed site call its own API without anyone remembering to add its hostname to ALLOWED_ORIGINS. A non-browser client can send both. It grants nothing curl does not already have by naming an allowed Origin directly, and no browser can be made to do it. Recorded so it is a known property rather than a discovery.
findings.evidence: lib/origin.ts, isOriginAllowed(): `if (new URL(origin).host === requestHost) return true;`
findings.remediation: No action. If the API ever gains an action worth protecting from scripted callers, the proof-of-work and rate limits are the layers that do it — not the Origin header, which any non-browser client sets freely.

results.describe: The Node service on 3100 and Redis on 6379 are not reachable from the public internet, which the runbook asserts and nothing else tests.
Directories that have no index page answer 403/404 rather than an Apache-generated file listing.
Live proof that /event and both /dns-leak routes refuse a foreign Origin and a missing Origin — the three routes security-smoke.mjs never probes.
The live certificate verifies, covers the served hostname, has more than 21 days left, and TLS 1.0/1.1 are refused.
The co-tenant WordPress at the shared web root is not receiving our noindex header, our CSP, or our 404 page.
A client-address header supplied by the caller does not become the IP the API rate-limits on.
Calls every route with a self-consistent forged Origin/Host pair and records which ones the allowlist lets through.

findings.title: The Origin allowlist is satisfied by a header pair the caller supplies
findings.detail: isOriginAllowed returns true whenever the Origin host equals the Host header, and with ProxyPreserveHost On the caller controls both. curl -H "Origin: https://evil.example" -H "Host: evil.example" is inside the gate on every route without knowing any allowlisted origin. Nothing here needs fixing for browsers — CORS still protects them — but the gate must not be counted as one of three layers against scripted abuse. The proof-of-work is the only layer that costs a script anything, which makes every finding about the PoW claim worth more than it looks.
findings.evidence: /challenge: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 200 (not 403) ; /scan-url: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 401 (not 403) ; /ip: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 200 (not 403) ; /dns-leak/start: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 200 (not 403) ; /dns-leak/result: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 400 (not 403) ; /event: Origin https://evil.example.test + Host evil.example.test → HTTP 400 (not 403)
findings.remediation: Either accept and document it (the current position — see the comment in lib/origin.ts), or compare against a configured canonical host instead of the request Host header.

results.describe: Runs /scan-url against an instrumented Redis and asserts the single-use claim is written, replays are refused, and a sick store fails closed.
Posts a 2 MiB chunked body to every route and counts the bytes each one pulled before answering.

findings.title: 4 routes buffer an entire chunked request body before refusing it
findings.detail: A POST with no Content-Length is read in full and only then measured against a cap of a few hundred bytes. The Apache <If "%{HTTP:Content-Length} -gt 1048576"> block cannot stop it — the expression is false when the header is absent — so nothing bounds the allocation but the service's own memory ceiling. The cheapest one is /dns-leak/result: origin + 100/min — the cheapest unauthenticated allocation path in the service. Repeated concurrently this is a memory-exhaustion path on a 768M-capped process sharing a box with MySQL and WordPress.
findings.evidence: /event (cap 2048 bytes, gate: origin + 120/min) → HTTP 413 after pulling 2097152 of 2097152 bytes ; /dns-leak/result (cap 512 bytes, gate: origin + 100/min — the cheapest unauthenticated allocation path in the service) → HTTP 413 after pulling 2097152 of 2097152 bytes ; /scan-url (cap 3072 bytes, gate: origin + proof-of-work + 10/min) → HTTP 413 after pulling 2097152 of 2097152 bytes ; /stats (cap 512 bytes, gate: bearer STATS_TOKEN, checked before the body) → HTTP 413 after pulling 2097152 of 2097152 bytes
findings.remediation: Either read the body as a stream and abort past the cap instead of awaiting request.text(), or record the decision and its compensating control in scripts/security/data/iast-body-bound-decisions.json.

results.describe: Drives the resolve-then-judge SSRF branch with a stubbed resolver and asserts no socket was opened for any blocked target.

results.describe: Every origin the WebView bridge contract hands the Android app is one lib/tiers.ts still serves from, and none is a subdomain someone else can re-register.
The live free site and a live Pro tool page serve an in-app boot script that runs, strips the app's flags from the address bar, and refuses a bare ?pro=1.
The app's visitor-supplied pro flag is read by an allowlisted set of modules only, and no page we build publishes a link that carries it.
saveImageInApp — the only path from this codebase to a native MediaStore write — is called from the one component we have reviewed for it.
Every payload field that reaches a Redis key name in eventKeys() is constrained by a finite Set, not by a slug regex — and the fan-out cap and TTL are still in source.
No upgrade gate guards anything that costs the server work or returns data the free tier does not hold, and the Pro signal still needs more than a query parameter.
The origin allowlists that live in documents — the WebView bridge set and the copy-paste CSP blocks — name only origins this project still controls, and do name the live one.
Unverified requests cannot spend the shared /24 rate-limit budget: the proof-of-work is checked before the limiter, or unverified traffic is charged to its own bucket.

findings.title: app/scan-url/route.ts spends the rate-limit budget before checking the proof-of-work
findings.detail: rateLimit() runs at line 90 and verifySolution() only at line 104, so a request carrying no solution at all still decrements the counter before it is refused. Because getIpBucket() collapses to a /24, one host can spend the allowance of everyone behind the same prefix at no CPU cost — which is precisely what the proof-of-work exists to prevent. Guarding the scan budget: 10/min per /24, and each scan holds a socket, a response buffer and an Apache worker.
findings.evidence: app/scan-url/route.ts: rateLimit( at line 90, verifySolution( at line 104; no separate unverified bucket name found in the file
findings.remediation: Verify the proof-of-work first (it is a local HMAC compare, far cheaper than the scan it guards), or charge unverified requests to their own tighter bucket so they cannot touch the real one.

findings.title: app/challenge/route.ts rate-limits without any proof-of-work in front of it
findings.detail: Every caller, solved or not, spends the challenge budget: 30/min per /24, which is what a real visitor needs to get a token at all. There is no puzzle on this route to put first, so the only lever is the size of the budget and the width of the bucket.
findings.evidence: app/challenge/route.ts:73 rateLimit( … ) with no verifySolution( in the file
findings.remediation: Keep the budget deliberately sized for this, and revisit if abuse shows up: a /24 bucket means one host spends a whole network's allowance.

results.describe: A live /challenge still hands out a proof-of-work drawn from at least the documented 100k search space — the one control that makes scripted abuse cost anything.
/stats refuses everything except the exact bearer, is actually configured on the live box, and its token is not in the git tree.

findings.title: The positive /stats leg did not run: no STATS_TOKEN in this environment
findings.detail: The route refuses anonymous and wrong-bearer requests, which is half the property. That the REAL token still works — that the owner can actually read the funnel — was not verified by this run.
findings.evidence: STATS_TOKEN unset (checked process.env); https://206-189-186-34.nip.io/api/stats answered 401 anonymously and 401 to a wrong bearer
findings.remediation: Run the nightly cadence with STATS_TOKEN exported to grade the positive leg and the git-tree leg.

results.describe: The upgrade CTAs the droplet is serving right now still resolve to our own Play listing — catches a fix that never reached the box.
Every upgrade CTA in the built sites resolves to the Play listing for our own package — asserted by destination, never by comparing a constant to itself.
A caller cannot move its own rate-limit bucket by sending X-Forwarded-For, cf-connecting-ip or x-real-ip at the live host.
The vhost still refuses >1 MiB bodies to /api/ before proxying them into the 768M-capped Node process.
The live /etc/ib-api.env holds usable tuning values and the two secrets whose absence breaks or disarms the API.
ufw is still up, logrotate still runs hourly, and the disk still has room — the three host controls that keep MySQL alive.
Redis is not evicting keys — an eviction silently turns single-use proof-of-work back into replayable proof-of-work.
ib-api restart count, OOM kills on the box, and the Redis fallback line — the three runtime events nothing currently records.
Runtime health of the Redis-backed controls is reachable and healthy — the diagnostic is wired up, and the live instance says Redis is really there.

findings.title: getRedisDiagnostic() is exported and never called — the API cannot report whether its own controls are on
findings.detail: REDIS_URL going missing or wrong in /etc/ib-api.env disables proof-of-work single-use, the shared rate limiter and /event counting, all three at once, with every response still 200. The function written to surface that is dead code, so nothing inside or outside the process can see it happen.
findings.evidence: lib/rate-limit.ts:94 defines getRedisDiagnostic(); grep across app/ lib/ finds 0 call sites, and app/stats/route.ts does not mention it.
findings.remediation: Add a `runtime` block to the POST handler in app/stats/route.ts: { ...getRedisDiagnostic(), inFlightScans, uptimeSec: process.uptime(), pid }. Keep lastError behind STATS_TOKEN — it can carry a connection string.

findings.title: The rate limiter computes which backend served a request, then throws it away
findings.detail: RateLimitResult documents `backend` as being surfaced to callers, but buildHeaders discards it. A silent fall from Redis to a per-process Map is therefore invisible in the response as well as in the logs — the two places anyone would look.
findings.evidence: lib/rate-limit.ts:179 is `void backend;`, while the docstring above RateLimitResult.backend says it is surfaced. Both are in the same file.
findings.remediation: Either emit the header (X-RateLimit-Backend) or correct the docstring. Emitting it is more useful: it makes the fallback observable from any response.

findings.title: The live half of this check did not run: no STATS_TOKEN
findings.detail: The source findings above stand, but the deployed instance was not asked whether Redis is currently configured for it.
findings.evidence: ctx.statsToken is null; target would have been POST https://206-189-186-34.nip.io/api/stats
findings.remediation: Add STATS_TOKEN to .secrets (the same value as in /etc/ib-api.env) or export it before the run.

results.describe: The memory/CPU/task ceilings that stop an API flood from OOM-killing the team’s MySQL are still loaded on ib-api.
Every tuning knob whose zero hangs or disarms the service still declares a floor, and the challenge loop is still bounded.
The co-hosted WordPress and both static sites still answer, and are not quietly getting slow.

findings.title: / needed a second attempt
findings.detail: The first connection failed and the retry succeeded. Recorded rather than hidden: one-off transport failures are usually a stale pooled socket, but a pattern of them is not.
findings.evidence: GET https://206-189-186-34.nip.io/ → first attempt "fetch failed", retry 200 in 923ms
findings.remediation: No action unless this appears on consecutive nights.

results.describe: Compares the CSP and the fixed security headers declared in next.config.ts against an exact expected set, offline, so a directive cannot gain or lose a source unnoticed.
Sweeps app/, lib/ and components/ for eval-class and raw-HTML sinks and fails any that is not named, with a reason, in scripts/security/data/sast-sink-allowlist.json.
Times the real scanner, screenshot-leak, email and link engines on hostile input at their real size caps, and fails a regex or an algorithm that goes superlinear.
Asserts the origin gate, the rate limit and (on /scan-url) the proof-of-work and its single-use claim all run before the handler reads a body or makes an outbound fetch.
Asserts every route handler that buffers a request body checks content-length against a numeric cap first, and re-checks the length after reading.
Asserts every dynamic page route pre-renders a fixed set of params, and that lib/content.ts validates each segment before joining it onto DATA_DIR.
Finds tests whose assertions can silently not run — an expect() inside a try with a swallowing catch, or a hardcoded file path that no longer resolves.
Feeds javascript:/data:/vbscript:/file: payloads through the real link-unwrapper and email-pixel decoders and fails if any non-http string surfaces as something the UI renders into an href or src.
A package gaining a postinstall runs as www-data on the WordPress box; every install script in the lockfile must be on the reviewed list.

findings.title: esbuild moved out of the production closure and still has an install script
findings.detail: It was reviewed as a production package and is now dev-only. Lower risk, but the allowlist is out of date and the next real move would be harder to spot.
findings.evidence: package-lock.json: "node_modules/esbuild" dev=true devOptional=false → inProdClosure=false; the allowlist records inProdClosure=true.
findings.remediation: Re-read the reason in the allowlist against the new placement, then update the entry.

results.describe: Every lockfile entry still resolves to the public registry with a sha512 integrity hash — no forks, tarballs or local paths.
npm audit signatures still verifies the installed tree against the registry keys — an INVALID signature means the tarball is not what npm published.
Third-party JS pasted into the static export never reaches package-lock.json; this reads the built HTML and chunks instead.

results.describe: Every advisory suppression names a fact about this codebase; this re-checks each fact and names the GHSAs a broken one re-activates.
No real secret value from .env or .secrets appears anywhere in out/ or .next/ before those are rsynced to production.
GitHub secret scanning and push protection are still enabled on this public repository.

findings.title: GitHub scanning for non-provider patterns is off
findings.detail: Provider patterns only match credentials with a recognisable prefix — sk-ant-, ghp_, AKIA. Two of the three secrets that actually gate this system have no prefix at all: ALTCHA_HMAC_KEY and STATS_TOKEN are generated with `openssl rand -hex 32` (API-ON-DROPLET.md), so they look like any other hex blob. Non-provider patterns are the setting that would notice one of those being committed. Low rather than high because it is noisier and this repo has other hex in it, but it is the difference between catching the two secrets that matter most and catching neither.
findings.evidence: gh api repos/davidshadrake-rl/incognitobrowser-pseo → private: false, security_and_analysis.secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns.status = disabled
findings.remediation: Settings → Code security → Secret scanning → "Non-provider patterns", or: gh api -X PATCH repos/davidshadrake-rl/incognitobrowser-pseo -f 'security_and_analysis[secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns][status]=enabled'

results.describe: Sweeps every blob in git history for credential-shaped strings — a secret removed in a later commit is still published.
next.config.ts `env:` inlines its values into the client bundle; every key there must be NEXT_PUBLIC_.
.env and .secrets stay git-ignored, and no credential-shaped file is tracked.
The static export ships no source maps, and next.config.ts does not turn them on.
No page, layout or component reads a non-public env var — BUILD_TARGET=static bakes those into published HTML.
